## Abstract

Solid-oxide fuel/electrolyzer cells are limited by a dearth of electrolyte materials with low Ohmic

loss and an incomplete understanding of the structure-property relationships that would enable the

rational design of better materials. Here, using epitaxial thin-film growth, synchrotron-based X-

ray diffraction, impedance spectroscopy, and density-functional theory, we delineate the impact of

structural parameters (i.e., unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations) on ionic conductivity in the

electrolyte La0.9Sr0.1Ga0.95Mg0.05O3-δ. As compared to the zero-strain (or bulk-like) state,

compressive strain reduces the unit-cell volume while maintaining large octahedral rotations,

resulting in a strong reduction of ionic conductivity, while tensile strain increases the unit-cell

volume while quenching octahedral rotations, resulting in a negligible effect on the ionic

conductivity. Calculations reveal that larger unit-cell volumes and octahedral rotations decrease

migration barriers and create low-energy migration pathways, respectively. The desired

combination of large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations is normally contraindicated, but

through the creation of superlattice structure we experimentally realize both expanded unit-cell

volume and strong octahedral rotations which results in an enhancement of the ionic conductivity

by ~250%. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the structure-transport relationships

in perovskite electrolytes and shed new light on the rational design of ion-conducting materials.

3

The need for high operation temperatures (>800°C) for solid-oxide fuel/electrolyzer cells

to reduce Ohmic loss has been one of the major limitations for commercialization.1–3 In an effort

to push the operating temperature down to a more cost-effective range (<500°C), considerable

research activities have been undertaken on the development of electrolytes with improved low-

temperature ionic conductivity.4,5 In this regard, doped-perovskite systems (i.e., A1-xA’xB1-yB’yO3-δ

where A’ and B’ are aliovalent dopants) have emerged as promising candidates for oxygen-ion

conductors.6 For example, strontium and magnesium co-doped LaGaO3 has been identified as an

excellent alternative to yttrium-stabilized zirconia due to its competitive ionic conductivity (>0.01

S.cm-1 at 600°C) and chemical stability.7–10 But, despite the attractive properties of this system, few

high-performance alternatives have been discovered11,12 and a systematic approach to the design

of such materials has yet to be established. This is made more difficult by the fact that most work

in this regard has focused on polycrystalline and mesostructured ceramics where extrinsic effects

(arising from, e.g., secondary phases and grain boundaries) are present.11,13–15 In turn, many of the

advances have come from the chemical and physical intuitions of researchers in the field and time-

consuming trial-and-error experimental iterations.

In order to advance a rational-design approach for ionic-conducting materials, it is vital to

gain a thorough understanding of the impact of systematic changes to the structure and chemistry

on property evolution. In this spirit, researchers have undertaken a range of studies on thin-film

versions of various ionic-conducting systems where lattice symmetry, microstructure, and material

stoichiometry can be deterministically controlled and studied.16–21 At the same time, advances in

theoretical understanding of these systems have provided suggestions as to how to manipulate the

structure so as to improve the transport properties.22,23 These initial studies, however, have provided,

at times, conflicting recommendations and outcomes. Such incongruous results are potentially


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

related to incomplete or limited structural characterization of the systems under study16,19 and from

confounding extrinsic contributions arising from sample geometry/structure (e.g., microstructure20,

substrate contributions to conductivity21,24, etc.). Additionally, most studies have focused on

fluorite structures while the more complex perovskite systems remain understudied. Thus, one key

to developing a rational-design approach for high ion-conducting perovskites is to quantitatively

and deterministically control the structural variables and build up a systematic correlation between

these variables and transport properties without convolution from extrinsic effects.

Here, we create a model perovskite ion-conducting system using thin-film epitaxy where

chemical inhomogeneity, grain boundaries, and secondary phases are absent. This multi-faceted

experimental and theoretical study delineates the impact of structural parameters (namely, unit-

cell volume and octahedral rotations) on ionic conductivity in the perovskite electrolyte

La0.9Sr0.1Ga0.95Mg0.05O3-δ. Films of this material were grown on a range of substrates producing

strain states from -1.12% to 1.10%. As compared to the zero-strain (or bulk-like) state,

compressive strain reduces the unit-cell volume while maintaining large octahedral rotations while

tensile strain increases the unit-cell volume while quenching octahedral rotations. In turn,

compressive and tensile strains are found to strongly reduce and have negligible effect on the ionic

conductivity, respectively. The resulting intuitive design recommendation is that both large unit-

cell volume and octahedral rotations are required for large ionic conductivity. Density-functional

theory (DFT) calculations reveal that larger unit-cell volumes and octahedral rotations decrease

migration-energy barriers and create a set of low-energy migration pathways, respectively. Unit-

cell volume and octahedral rotations are strongly coupled and often contraindicated, but this

limitation can be overcome via superlattice structuring which enables the creation of both large

unit-cell volumes and octahedral rotations which drives a subsequent enhancement of the ionic


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

conductivity by nearly 250% as compared to the compressively strained heterostructures.

Ultimately, these findings provide a strong indication of the structure-transport relationships in the

perovskite system and shed new light on how one can rationally design novel high-performance

electrolytes.

100 nm La0.9Sr0.1Ga0.95Mg0.05O3-δ (LSGM)/NdGaO3 (110), SrTiO3 (001), and DyScO3 (110)

heterostructures were grown via pulsed-laser deposition (Methods) corresponding to lattice

mismatches of -1.12%, +0.05%, and +1.10%, respectively (where “-” and “+” indicate

compressive and tensile strain, respectively). The resulting (001)pc-oriented heterostructures

(where pc refers to pseudocubic indices) are found to be single-phase and highly-crystalline

(Supplementary Figure 1a). Additionally, reciprocal space mapping studies (Methods) of the

LSGM heterostructures along two orthogonal in-plane directions reveal that the films are

coherently strained on all substrates (Figure 1a and Supplementary Figure 1b-c). The stoichiometry

of the LSGM films was characterized via Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS, Methods)

and the film chemistries were found to be La0.9Sr0.1Ga0.95Mg0.05O3-δ (Supplementary Figure 1d).

This is further supported by biaxial-strain lattice calculations where the expected bulk lattice

parameter (i.e., the pseudocubic lattice parameter averaged over three orthogonal axes) of LSGM

is acquired for each strain state (Supplementary Figure 1e). All told, the LSGM heterostructures

are of the same chemistry and coherently strained to the various substrates and complete

understanding of the LSGM lattice parameters and unit-cell volumes can be extracted.

Synchrotron-based half-order Bragg peak analysis (Methods) is applied to further examine

the octahedral rotation evolution under epitaxial constraint. Briefly, the octahedral rotations in a

perovskite unit-cell decrease the lattice symmetry and give rise to half-order diffraction peaks of

which the intensities are related to the magnitudes of the oxygen-anion displacement. For instance,


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

a representative 1/2 1/2 3/2-diffraction peak for the LSGM/SrTiO3 (001) heterostructure is shown

(at 25°C and 650°C), indicating that octahedral rotations are present in the system and that the

magnitude of the rotation is similar across the temperature range of our studies (Figure 1b). In turn,

a systematic fitting of characteristic half-order Bragg peaks intensities (Supplementary Figure 2)

reveals the angles by which the octahedra rotate along each orthogonal direction (i.e., α, β, and γ

along [100]pc, [010]pc, and [001]pc, respectively).25–27 Thus, from both the reciprocal space mapping

and half-order Bragg peak analysis studies, the structural parameters of the LSGM heterostructures

and corresponding changes induced by epitaxial strain can be quantitatively extracted (Figure 1c

and Supplementary Table 1). Note, for simplicity of presentation, in later discussions we define an

effective octahedral rotation magnitude as "𝛼$ + 𝛽$ + 𝛾$. To summarize the observations, in

comparison to the zero-strain state (i.e., on the SrTiO3 substrates, where the extracted structural

parameters are in excellent agreement with bulk crystals28–30), as we progress from compressive to

tensile strain, the unit-cell volume of LSGM increases monotonically. Additionally, while the

octahedral rotations are found to be the largest near the zero-strain state, they are slightly quenched

under compressive strain, and almost fully suppressed under tensile strain (Figure 1d where

projection along [001]pc is shown).

With this detailed understanding of the structural evolution, we proceed to correlate these

structural changes with the ionic transport. To characterize ion-transport properties in the LSGM

thin films, in-plane AC-impedance spectroscopy measurements are performed on all

heterostructures from 500°C to 650°C under high (pure O2) and low (pure N2) oxygen-partial

pressures (Methods). For brevity, representative Nyquist plots, taken at 500°C, are provided

(Figure 2a-c), but data across the full measured temperature range are available (Supplementary

*Figure 3a-c). All heterostructures show one dominant “waterdrop-like” capacitive feature which*

7

arises from chemical capacitance of the diffusing charges (i.e., electrons and ions),31,32 and also

indicates that the platinum electrodes are essentially blocking with negligible gas reaction at the

triple-phase-boundaries. Additionally, strong oxygen-partial pressure dependence of impedance at

low frequency (electronic impedance  𝑍) ) reveals limited p-type electronic conduction. The

invariant high-frequency impedance (where total impedance 𝑍*+*,- = 𝑍) + 𝑍/, where 𝑍/ is the

ionic impedance) under different oxygen-partial pressures confirms the ionic charge concentration

is fixed by extrinsic doping, and that the conduction in the heterostructures is dominated by the

LSGM thin films. To further rule out substrate contributions to the total conduction, measurements

on bare substrates were also performed (Supplementary Figure 4a-c). The NdGaO3 and DyScO3

substrates show negligible mixed ionic and electronic conductance while the SrTiO3 substrates

show dominant p-type electronic conduction which will not affect the ionic conduction extracted

from the heterostructures.33

The ionic conductivity of the LSGM is determined by fitting the impedance spectra using

a transmission line model developed for mixed ionic and electronic conductors (Supplementary

*Figure 5a-c). Fitting reveal a high ion-charge-transfer number (𝑡=*

12314

12 × 100%, where 𝜎: and

𝜎)are the total and electronic conductivity, respectively) of 94-98% across all heterostructures

(Figure 2d), consistent with results for single-crystal LSGM samples.10 The smaller ion-charge-

transfer number in the LSGM/SrTiO3 heterostructures is expected due to the relatively high

electronic conduction from the SrTiO3 substrates. In turn, we can extract the strain- and

temperature-dependent evolution of the ionic conductivity and the migration-energy barrier for all

heterostructures (Figure 2e). Examination of the conductivity and the structural parameters reveals

several key findings. First, the migration-energy barrier is found to be similar for all

heterostructures (𝐸, = 0.70 ± 0.05 𝑒𝑉). Second, the conductivity of the near-zero strain state


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

heterostructure matches well with values measured for bulk single-crystal samples (e.g., the

conductivity at 600°C for our films and bulk samples are 0.0126 S/cm and 0.0128  S/cm10,

respectively). Third, the structural changes in LSGM are revealed to have a significant impact on

the ion-transport properties. In particular, from compressive strain to near-zero strain, as the

LSGM unit-cell volume increases by ~1% while the octahedral-rotation magnitude remains almost

invariant, the conductivity of the LSGM is increased by ~100%, indicating that a larger unit-cell

volume is preferred to achieve high ionic conductivity. Moreover, as the unit-cell volume is further

increased by another ~1% under tensile strain, while simultaneously quenching the octahedral

rotations, the observed conductivity is negligibly affected (increases by <5%). This suggests that

quenching the octahedral rotations also strongly affects the overall transport properties, thus

counterbalancing the effect of the expanded unit cell under tensile strain. In other words, strain-

induced changes in the unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations both have significant impact on

ionic conductivity. In turn, to achieve high ionic conduction in perovskite structures, it is implied

that the material should be designed to have both large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations.

To understand why these structural features impact ionic conductivity in this manner, we

applied DFT calculations coupled with a Green’s function method34 to probe the local effect of

structure on ion transport (Methods). The undoped LaGaO3 parent phase was first examined to

study the impact of octahedral rotations on ion-migration pathways, and at the same time to

eliminate the dopant strain effects. Because of the distorted octahedra in LaGaO3, there are two

distinct oxygen sites located either in the LaO or GaO2 planes; we denote these sites as O1 and O2,

respectively (Figure 3a and Supplementary Figure 6a). Calculations further support this difference

in that the energy of a vacancy at an O1 site is 15 meV lower than that for a vacancy at an O2 site.

Furthermore, due to the octahedral rotations,35,36 it is found that there are two O1-O1-type and four


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

O1-O2-type symmetry-unique vacancy jumps with distinct migration-energy barriers (noted in

various colors, bottom Figure 3a). Since there are no allowed O2-O2-type jumps, vacancy

migration along the three orthogonal axes (i.e., in-plane [001] and [11G0], and out-of-plane [110])

is achieved by either a series of O1-O1-type jumps or a combination of O1-O1 and O1-O2-type

jumps. As a result, compared to cubic system with no octahedral rotations, the presence of

octahedral rotations creates different energy barrier to ion migration along each direction and, in

turn, anisotropic jump phenomena. Thus ion conduction preferentially occurs along a sub-set of

low-energy jumps thereby resulting in two types of fast ion-conducting pathways: The first is via

a series of O1-O1-type jumps (two equivalent pathways along different directions are shown,

*Figure 3b) and the second is via a series of O1-O1 and O1-O2-type jumps (Figure 3c). In general,*

the O1-O1-type jump with the highest energy (0.35 eV) determines the overall migration-energy

barrier. We note that this value is smaller than that extracted from the experiments (~0.70 eV) and

this discrepancy will be addressed later. Having established the nature of jump phenomena in

unstrained LaGaO3, bi-axial strain (compressive -2% to tensile +2%) was subsequently applied to

examine the impact of unit-cell volume change. In undoped LaGaO3, the unit-cell volume is shown

to expand by ~8% from compressive to tensile strain while the octahedral rotations remain almost

unchanged (< 2° change in angles across this entire range of strain) (Supplementary Figure 6b),

and therefore, the impact of unit-cell volume can be isolated. Diffusivity calculations reveal that,

from compressive to tensile strain, the ionic diffusivity is nearly isotropic and increases by two

orders of magnitude (Figure 3d). This enhancement of the diffusivity under tensile strain is a direct

consequence of a strain-induced reduction in all jump energy barriers in the expanded unit cells

(Supplementary Figure 6c) and confirms the experimental findings that a larger unit-cell volume

is preferred for higher ionic conduction.


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

For a better representation of the experimental scenario, both strontium- and magnesium-

doped versions of LaGaO3 were also examined. These studies reveal that the nearest strontium-

on-a-lanthanum sites (Sr1) have attractive binding with both vacancy sites (O1 and O2) while the

nearest magnesium-on-a-gallium sites (Mg1) have negligible repulsive binding with the vacancies

(Supplementary Figure 7a, b). In other words, this suggests that while strontium acts as a trap for

vacancy diffusion, the magnesium has little to no effect. In turn, to examine the rate-limiting steps

for vacancy diffusion, the oxygen-vacancy-migration barriers out of the most strongly bounded

O1-Sr1 and O2-Sr1 vacancy configurations were calculated (Figure 3e). Vacancies are found to

either jump between bound sites (i.e., they circle around the strontium trap) through low-energy

barrier jumps (0.20-0.45 eV) or jump towards unbound sites (i.e., escape from the strontium trap)

through high-energy barrier jumps (0.61-0.80 eV). The energies required for the vacancy to jump

out of the trap, therefore, is likely to control the diffusion behavior in doped systems. Thus, with

the inclusion of dopant effects, the escape energies from O1 and O2 sites (0.61 eV and 0.65 eV)

agree well with the experimentally observed activation barriers (~0.70 eV). Once again, now

building from both experimental and theoretical findings, the optimal design for high ion-

conducting perovskites is to combine large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations.

As such, we now turn our attention to creating such an optimal structure wherein we can

demonstrate the efficacy of this design process. To do this, we turn to a combined strain and

interfacial engineering approach25,37. Although a particular rotation pattern of an epitaxial film is

energetically fixed under a given strain state38,39, it has been shown that utilization of perovskite

substrates with large octahedral rotations can drive an increase in the rotation magnitude in the

film near the heterointerface (Figure 4a)25,37,40,41. Thus, in order to achieve both large unit-cell

volume and octahedral rotations in the LSGM, we turn to superlattice structures of


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

(LSGM)n/(DyScO3)m (where n and m refer to the number of unit cells (UC) of LSGM and DyScO3,

respectively) grown on DyScO3 substrate (Figure 4b). The superlattice structure is chosen for a

number of reasons. First, DyScO3 is an insulating material with large octahedral rotations (the

scandium-oxygen-scandium bonding angle is ~140°)42,43 such that the rotation pattern from the

DyScO3 interlayers can propagate into the LSGM layers from both the bottom and top interfaces.

Second, DyScO3 substrates are chosen to maintain the desired tensile strain across the superlattice

structure such that the unit-cell volume of LSGM is expanded. Finally, multiple LSGM layers give

rise to higher total conduction to limit the substrate contribution to conductivity and facilitate

easier measurement of the ion-transport properties.

(LSGM)n/(DyScO3)m superlattices (n = 6-10 UC, m = 6 UC) were prepared via reflection

high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED)-assisted pulsed-laser deposition (Figure 4c). X-ray

diffraction studies of the heterostructures reveal strong superlattice peaks with clear Laue fringes,

indicating high crystallinity and sharp interfaces (Figure 4d). The high crystallinity and interface

quality are also validated by sharp in situ RHEED patterns during the growth (insets, Figure 4c).

Additionally, the superlattice structures are found to be coherently strained to the substrate via

reciprocal space mapping studies (Supplementary Figure 8a) and structurally and chemically

robust during ~24 hours of high-temperature measurement (Supplementary Figure 8b). To confirm

the realization of the desired large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations in the LSGM,

synchrotron-based X-ray coherent Bragg rod analysis (COBRA) was performed on a 6 UC

DyScO3/6 UC LSGM/DyScO3 (110) emulating a single repeat of the superlattice structures.

COBRA allows for the extraction of atomic positions for each layer of the structure near the surface

(approximately the top 20 nm of the heterostructure). Although the rotation magnitude of thicker

LSGM films under tensile strain is nearly zero, the electron density maps projected along the [001]


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

(the projection along [11G0] is also provided, Supplementary Figure 8c) clearly reveal large tilts of

the octahedra in the ultrathin LSGM layer embedded between the DyScO3 layers (Figure 4e). Both

DyScO3 layers also show large and rigid octahedral rotation patterns and the extracted octahedral

rotation angles are in good agreement with bulk values42,43. The extracted octahedral rotations for

the 6 UC LSGM layer are, however, drastically different from bulk values30 (Figure 4f). Namely,

the two in-plane rotation angles (𝛼 and 𝛽) are increased due to the coupling with the DyScO3 layers

while the out-of-plane rotation angle (𝛾) is quenched as a result of the tensile strain. Overall,

compared to the 100-nm-thick LSGM grown directly on DyScO3 substrates where the octahedral

rotations are significantly quenched, the effective octahedral rotation magnitude for the ultrathin

LSGM in the superlattice structures has been dramatically increased from ~2.3° to ~13.7°.

Having demonstrated that the superlattice produces the desired effect on the crystal

structure, impedance measurements were completed (Supplementary Figure 9a). To ultimately

extract the ionic conductivity of this optimal structure in the superlattice geometery, we have two

challenges: First is to assure that all LSGM layers are conducting and, second, is to have accurate

values of the thickness of the conducting layers. To accomplish this, we take advantage of our

ability to grow various superlattice structures and periodicities, to apply standard scaling laws to

the analysis of the data. To confirm that all LSGM layers in the superlattices were conducting, we

examined a representative (LSGM)6/(DyScO3)6 superlattice structure with different total

thicknesses (i.e., 8 and 16 total repetitions) and it was found that the normalized impedance was

the same (Supplementary Figure 9b), thus confirming that all layers do conduct. As it pertains to

understanding the thickness of the conducting layers, because there is a lack of complete

understanding about the nature of ionic conduction at and near interfaces, we make no assumption

at each of the LSGM UC is conducting in the same fashion. In turn, we assume the average

conducting LSGM UC to be 𝑛−Δ, where Δ denotes potentially non-conducting UC at/near

interfaces (Supplementary Figure 9c). As such, a linear relationship between the reciprocal of total

region of interest (500°C to 650°C) yields 𝑍H and subsequently the conductivity of the LSGM can

be extracted (Supplementary Figure 9d, e). We observe that there is an invariant number of non-

conducting LSGM “dead layers” (Δ ≈5). We attribute this observation to strontium enrichment

near the top of the ultrathin LSGM layers as has been probed via low-energy ion scattering

(Methods and Supplementary Figure 9f,g). The higher concentration of strontium could exacerbate

trapping of oxygen vacancies and impede migration. With this noted, we extracted the conductivity

of our optimized perovskite structure (with both large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations)

and find that it is increased by ~250% as compared to the non-optimal, compressively-strain

heterostructures and nearly 70% as compared to the bulk-like state (Figure 5). This result suggests

that the design algorithm revealed by this work can provide a pathway to greatly enhance the ionic-

transport properties.

In summary, the correlation between structural features (i.e., unit-cell volume and

octahedral rotations) and ionic conductivity in perovskite oxides has been investigated.

Quantifiable control over unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations in LSGM was achieved via

strain engineering. It was found that unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations both have significant

impact on ionic migration in the perovskite structure and the optimal design is to have both large

unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations. DFT calculations of vacancy diffusion further reveal

that larger unit-cell volume reduces migration-energy barriers while large octahedral rotations

create low-energy migration pathways. Subsequent superlattice structuring enables the creation of

both large unit-cell volume and octahedral rotations which ultimately result in nearly a 250%

increase in conductivity. Again, this work reveals the detailed relationships between structural

parameters and transport evolution in perovskite ion-conducting systems and provides insights

towards a rational-design approach of electrolyte materials for intermediate-temperature energy

conversion applications.

## Methods

Thin-film synthesis. A ceramic target of La0.9Sr0.1Ga0.9Mg0.1O3-δ, with 95% theoretical

density, was used for film growth. 100-nm-thick LSGM thin films were grown via pulsed-laser

deposition (PLD) on NdGaO3 (110), SrTiO3 (001), and DyScO3 (110) substrates (CrysTec, GmBH).

The LSGM films was grown at a heater temperature of 800°C in a dynamic oxygen pressure of 40

mTorr and with a laser fluence and repetition rate of 1.8 J/cm2 and 5 Hz, respectively. All films

were grown in an on-axis geometry with a target-to-substrate distance of 52 mm. Following growth,

the films were cooled to room temperature at a rate of 10°C/min. in a static oxygen pressure of

700 Torr. Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED)-assisted PLD is used to synthesize

the superlattice structures. Same growth conditions were used for both LSGM and DyScO3 layers

except that the laser repetition rate was adjusted to 2 and 3 Hz, respectively, for better visualization

of RHEED oscillations.

X-ray diffraction studies. A high-resolution X-ray diffractometer (Panalytical, X’Pert3

MRD) was used to perform line scans and reciprocal space mapping studies about the 013pc- and

103pc-diffraction conditions for cubic substrates and 332- and 420-diffraction conditions for

orthorhombic substrates. Strain-dependent and high-temperature synchrotron-based X-ray half-

order Bragg peak analysis was conducted at the Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National

Laboratory, Sector 33-ID-D and sector 33-BM-C, respectively. Odd-odd-odd, odd-odd-even, and

odd-even-even types of half-order peaks were systematically scanned in all four quadrants in

reciprocal space and the peak intensities are integrated and corrected according to instrumental

geometry. The peak intensities are subsequently fitted using an established approach for Pbnm

perovskites and the octahedral rotation patterns and angles are extracted.27 Coherent Bragg rod

analysis (COBRA) studies were completed at the Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

Laboratory, Sector 12-ID-D. Crystal truncation rods (CTRs) were measured using a surface X-ray

diffraction geometry with a six-circle diffractometer under X-ray photon energy of 16 keV with a

total flux of ~2.0×1012 photons/sec. The two-dimensional diffraction images of CTRs at each L

step in the reciprocal space were recorded with a pixel array area detector (Dectris PILATUS 100

K). Samples were protected under dry helium gas flow in a concealed sample cell during room

temperature measurements. A large set of CTRs in the reciprocal lattice coordinate were measured

for 6ML DyScO3/6ML LSGM/DyScO3 heterostructure at room temperature with Hmax, Kmax= 4 r.l.u.

and Lmax= 9 r.l.u. under 2×2×2 pseudo-cubic notation.

Rutherford backscattering spectrometry. The film chemistry was probed ex situ using

Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (incident ion energy 3.3 MeV, incident angle α = 22.5°,

exit angle β = 25.35°, and scattering angle θ = 168°) and the spectra were fitted using the RBS

analysis software SIMNRA. The beam energy was specifically tuned around Mg resonance to

maximize the scattering cross section for this light element.44,45

Impedance-spectroscopy studies. Impedance studies were completed with a PARSTAT

3000A Potentiostat (Princeton Applied Research) and impedance spectra were fitted using ZView

software (Solartron Analytical). Transport measurements were performed by sputtering 120-nm-

thick platinum interdigitated electrodes (8 μm spacing, 500 μm arm length) and subsequently gold-

wire-bonded to a Ceramic Dual In-line Package (CerDIP, TopLine Corp.) chip carrier. Samples

are sealed inside an alumina tube. Electrical connections from CerDIP to the customized

feedthroughs at one end of the tube are made via silver wires electrically/thermally insulated by

ceramic beads. A K-type thermocouple is mounted on the CerDIP and wired out from the

customized feedthrough for temperature readout. To achieve different oxygen partial pressures,

the alumina tube was first pumped down to vacuum and then flushed with oxygen or nitrogen gas


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

(Praxair Inc.) with 99.99% purity. A constant oxygen or nitrogen gas flow, with flow rate of 30

ml/min (monitored by two separate flowmeters), was maintained during measurement.

Density-functional theory (DFT). The DFT calculations are performed using PBE

exchange-correlation functional and the PAW method implemented in VASP. Lanthanum,

Strontium, Gallium, Magnesium, and Oxygen atoms are described with electronic structure

5s25p65d16s2, 4s24p65s2, 3d104s24p1, 2p63s2, and 2s22p4, respectively. A plane wave energy cut-off

of 500 eV is used to converge the total energy of the LaGaO3 unit-cell to below 1 meV/atom. The

supercell of LaGaO3 consists 160 atoms with a size of 2 × 2 × 2 and requires a Monkhorst-Pack

k-point mesh size of 4× 4 × 2 to sample the Brillouin Zone. The density of states is integrated via

Gaussian smearing with an energy smearing width of 0.2 eV. The convergence criterion for

electronic minimization is an energy difference smaller than 10-8 eV and the geometries are relaxed

using conjugate gradient until the force on each atom is less than 5 meV/Å. Climbing image NEB

method with a single image is used to determine the transition states for vacancy jumps.
